name: Kingdom of Castile
summary: A Christian kingdom in central Spain that led the Reconquista; joined with León in 1230 and with Aragon through the marriage of Isabella and Ferdinand (1469), it conquered Granada and sent Columbus west in 1492.

knownFor.label: Merino wool
knownFor.note: Fine wool from sheep herds (the Mesta).

location.value: A polity in the Iberian Peninsula in the Middle Ages, now part of Spain.

terrain.value: Mostly the high Meseta plateau, crossed by the Duero and Tagus rivers and ringed by mountains such as the Cantabrian range and the Guadarrama.

climate.value: Continental on the Meseta, with hot, dry summers and cold winters; milder and wetter on the northern coast and hotter in Andalusia.

resources.value: Merino wool from huge sheep flocks, grain from the Meseta, iron from Biscay, and olive oil and wine from Andalusia.

disasters.value: The Black Death (1348–50) killed King Alfonso XI during the siege of Gibraltar in 1350; plague and famine returned later.

population.value: About 3 million around 1300, up from about 1 million earlier. The page gives no figure for 1500.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural; a few walled towns and a royal or ducal capital.

disease.value: Plague outbreaks, above all the Black Death (1347–51).

migration.value: Settlers moved south as land was conquered.

economicBase.value: Moorish rule had made Castile’s high central plateau a vast sheep pasturage; the page does not mention the Mesta or wool exports.

tradeRoutes.value: Wool to Flanders through Burgos and Bilbao.

wealth.value: Wool exports, Andalusian farms and tribute (parias) once taken from Muslim kingdoms enriched the crown and great nobles.

moneyAndTax.value: The maravedí, first a gold coin and later a unit of account; the alcabala sales tax and other taxes voted by the Cortes.

inequality.value: Nobles and clergy above peasants, many of them serfs.

governmentType.value: Had no settled capital, according to the infobox.

keyRulers.value: The Catholic Monarchs: marriage at Valladolid in 1469; personal union of the Crowns in 1479.

succession.value: Hereditary, and women could inherit, as Urraca and Isabella I did; disputes caused civil wars, as in 1366–69 and 1475–79.

institutions.value: The Cortes, royal councils, the Siete Partidas law code of Alfonso X (about 1265), and the Santa Hermandad police force (1476).

stability.value: Frequent noble revolts and civil wars, including the war between Peter I and Henry of Trastámara (1366–69) and strife under Henry IV.

eliteConflict.value: Great noble families such as the Lara and later the Mendoza fought the kings and each other, especially in the 1300s and 1400s.

majorWars.value: Castile conquered Granada, the last Moorish state, in 1492, ending Muslim rule in Iberia; the page gives no dates for Las Navas de Tolosa or Seville.

territoryChange.value: Took Toledo (1085), most of Andalusia including Córdoba (1236) and Seville (1248), Murcia, and finally Granada (1492).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals of Portugal, Aragon, Navarre and Granada; allied with France in the Hundred Years’ War, and joined to Aragon by Isabella and Ferdinand’s marriage (1469).

inventions.value: No major inventions, but the Toledo School of Translators turned Arabic science and philosophy into Latin and Castilian.

scienceEducation.value: The University of Salamanca (founded 1218), cathedral schools, and the Toledo translators, who passed Arabic learning to Latin Europe.

openness.value: Open to trade; closed to rival faiths at times.

communicationTransport.value: Old Roman roads, mule trains and the Mesta’s sheep tracks (cañadas) across the Meseta, with coastal shipping from Biscay and Seville.

religion.value: Roman Catholic, with Muslim and Sephardic Jewish minorities. In 1492 the monarchs decided that Jews who would not convert must leave; the page estimates 50,000 to 70,000 were expelled from Castile.

languageWriting.value: Castilian Spanish, which Alfonso X made a language of law and scholarship; Antonio de Nebrija published the first Castilian grammar in 1492.

socialStructure.value: Nobles, clergy, towns, peasants; Muslim and Jewish minorities.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the crown, the Catholic faith and the crusading Reconquista, alongside strong local and town identities.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; bread, porridge and beer or wine.

neighbours.value: Aragon, Navarre and Portugal, the Muslim kingdom of Granada to the south, and France across the western Pyrenees.

colonisation.value: Conquered the Canary Islands (1402–96) and, after Columbus’s voyage of 1492, began settling Hispaniola and other Caribbean islands.

riseSignals.value: The name Castile first appears in a document of AD 800; Rodrigo is named as first count in 850; it became a separate kingdom from León in 1065.

peakPeriod.value: Isabella I succeeded her brother and died in 1504; her 1469 marriage to Ferdinand II of Aragon began a union of the two kingdoms, which became a personal union after Ferdinand succeeded in Aragon in 1479. The page does not give 1474 as the start of her reign.

declineSignals.value: No real decline; after Isabella’s death (1504) it passed to her daughter Joanna and merged into Spain under Charles I (1516).

outcome.value: Permanent union with León from 23 September 1230. Toledo was taken in 1085 and Granada in 1492. The Crowns of Castile and Aragon were united in a personal union in 1479.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and charters; population figures are estimates.
